issues.description: 14 chains per treatment is a relatively small sample size for detecting the subtle effects of transmitted causal theories on a multi-generational process, especially given the high variance in individual human behavior.
issues.quote: We collected data from 14 chains of 5 participants in this "Configurations" treatment.

issues.description: 5 trials per participant is extremely low for exploring a search space of 20,736 unique configurations. This likely forces participants to rely almost exclusively on social information, artificially suppressing the role of individual causal reasoning.
issues.quote: Each participant had 5 trials to minimize the time it took for the wheel to reach the end of the track.

issues.description: A 10-item binary choice test is a weak proxy for 'causal understanding.' With a 50% chance of guessing correctly, the resolution to detect subtle changes in understanding is very low, and the baseline scores (4.6/10) are already at chance levels.
issues.quote: The test comprised 10 pairs of wheels: 5 in which wheels varied in their moment of inertia, 5 in which wheels varied in the position of their centre of mass.

issues.description: The authors conclude that theory transmission has 'no noticeable effect,' but this may be a Type II error. The study may lack the statistical power or the necessary number of generations to observe the divergence between treatments.
issues.quote: we find that the transmission of causal models across generations has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution.

issues.description: Transmitting only the last two configurations and scores limits the 'fossil record' of the previous participant's search process. This prevents learners from seeing what failed, which is a critical component of causal learning.
issues.quote: All participants (except those in the first generation) were provided with the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in their chain

issues.description: Limiting written theories to 340 characters may artificially prevent the transmission of complex, multi-dimensional causal models, biasing the results toward the 'simplistic' models the authors then critique.
issues.quote: Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with “The wheel covers the distance faster when...”

issues.description: The failure of the preregistered model to converge suggests that the data structure was too complex for the sample size or that the negative correlation between inertia and CoM understanding violated model assumptions.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score

issues.description: Rewarding participants based on the next person's performance introduces a 'teaching' incentive. This might lead participants to simplify their theories to be 'helpful' rather than accurate, distorting the natural transmission of knowledge.
issues.quote: their reward depended both on their own performance and on the performance of the next participant in the chain.

issues.description: The wheel system is a closed physical system with a single optimal solution. Real-world technologies (like bows or kayaks) involve multi-objective trade-offs where causal reasoning is often used to balance competing needs (e.g., speed vs. stability).
issues.quote: the optimization problem is low-dimensional, which provides a conservative test of our hypotheses

issues.description: Presenting the 10 test pairs in the same order for all participants can introduce systematic bias due to fatigue or learning effects during the test itself.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.description: The use of French university students (a WEIRD population) limits the generalizability of the findings to the 'cultural niche' hypothesis, which is primarily concerned with human evolution in small-scale, traditional societies.
issues.quote: successive ‘cultural generations’ of participants (French university students)

issues.description: The use of sex-segregated chains is mentioned but not theoretically justified. Furthermore, the claim that results generalize to mixed-gender settings is an overstatement not supported by the experimental data.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.description: The average speed reached 145.7 m/h while the maximum was 154 m/h. This proximity to the ceiling (71% optimization in 4 generations) may have reduced the variance necessary to see any potential benefits of theory transmission.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.description: The study equates 'explicit causal understanding' with the ability to verbalize a theory or pass a binary test, ignoring the possibility of 'implicit' or 'procedural' causal knowledge that guides exploration.
issues.quote: in the absence of explicit causal understanding.

issues.description: 5 generations is a very short window for 'cultural evolution.' Many cumulative effects in technology, particularly those involving complex causal models, may require dozens of generations to manifest.
issues.quote: Participants were organized into chains of 5 individuals.

issues.description: The analysis of physics/engineering background is likely underpowered. If only a small percentage of the 140 students had this background, the 'no effect' finding is unreliable.
issues.quote: although physics or engineering background had no effect on participants’ understanding scores

issues.description: The experimenter was not blind to the conditions and could see the participants' configurations. This could lead to subtle cues or biases during the manual physical setup of the wheel for each trial.
issues.quote: the experimenter to see the chosen configuration without interacting with the participant

issues.description: The 'Configurations' treatment is not a pure 'no-understanding' control. Participants must use some form of logic or causal intuition to choose weights; the study lacks a 'random' or 'blind' transmission control.
issues.quote: This confirms that the retention of improvements over generations produces highly optimized solutions and need not depend on the emergence of more accurate causal models.

issues.description: The negative correlation between inertia and CoM understanding suggests that participants were 'specializing' their attention rather than failing to understand. Aggregating these scores masks this cognitive trade-off.
issues.quote: analyses revealed that understanding scores about inertia and centre of mass were negatively correlated

issues.description: Participants receive immediate, high-fidelity feedback (speed) after every trial. This 'hill-climbing' signal is so strong that it likely makes any transmitted theory redundant for the specific task provided.
issues.quote: The wheel’s average speed and associated payoff was then automatically displayed on the participant’s screen.

issues.description: The manuscript mentions 'wheels that did not descend' (failures) but does not provide a statistical analysis of whether theory transmission reduced the frequency of these catastrophic failures over time.
issues.quote: Vertical bars show the number of wheels that did not descend (i.e. failures) at each trial in each treatment.

issues.description: The authors argue optimization happens without causal understanding, yet admit participants had 'appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration.' These intuitions are themselves a form of causal knowledge.
issues.quote: This indicates that participants had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration

issues.description: The use of 12 discrete positions simplifies the search space significantly compared to real-world tool-making, potentially overestimating the efficiency of 'blind' optimization.
issues.quote: Weights could be placed on one of 12 discrete positions along 4 spokes

issues.description: The first generation's understanding score (4.60) is already below the chance level (5.0). This creates a floor effect where it is statistically difficult to show a 'lack of improvement' because there was no understanding to begin with.
issues.quote: their understanding score was 4.60 (95% HPDI: (3.83, 5.53)).

issues.description: Allowing participants to consult social information 'all along the building phase' might lead to mimicry before any individual attempt at understanding, confounding the two processes.
issues.quote: Social information was available all along the building phase and could be consulted between any trials in both treatments.
